extracted.intended_audience: general readers and urban reformers / municipal officials interested in tenement conditions and public-health policy
extracted.subtask_description: First-hand investigative reportage on late-19th-century New York slums, tenement overcrowding, lodging-houses, and police/health responses; aimed at documenting conditions to motivate reform. Focuses on descriptive metrics, official standards, and enforcement practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breathing-space requirement (health officers)
rubrics_metrics.description: The standard of breathing space required for an adult by the health officers has been cut down from six to four hundred cubic feet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as an official measurable standard for health/sanitary adequacy of living quarters; author uses the change (reduction) to argue that standards are being relaxed under pressure from population influxes (e.g., Italian immigrants), and that such relaxation strengthens the reformers' case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overcrowding: relative definition / sliding official scale
rubrics_metrics.description: The term overcrowding is a relative one, and the scale of official measurement conveniently sliding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrasts two counts: an official figure 'a little vaguely at four or five hundred' overcrowded houses versus a reformer assertion that there are 'thirty-two thousand' houses classed as tenements. Usefulness: indicates that legal/administrative definitions and measurements of overcrowding vary and can understate the problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apartment/vacancy counts as measure of overcrowding
rubrics_metrics.description: In 'the Bend' district ... a total of four thousand three hundred and sixty-seven 'apartments' only nine were for the moment vacant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses apartment counts and vacancy rates within a district to demonstrate extreme occupancy pressure and de facto homelessness; implies vacancy rate is a concrete metric to assess housing scarcity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Health Department / sanitary enforcement practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Through the long summer days their carts patrol 'the Bend,' scattering disinfectants in streets and lanes, in sinks and cellars, and hidden hovels ... From midnight till far into the small hours of the morning the policeman's thundering rap on closed doors is heard, with his stern command, 'Apri port'!' on his rounds gathering evidence of illegal overcrowding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes methods used by health and police authorities to detect and remediate unsanitary conditions and illegal overcrowding: patrols with disinfectants, surprise night inspections, forcible entry orders, and photographic documentation. Suggests these are operational standards of enforcement rather than preventive solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanitary police vaccination practice
rubrics_metrics.description: In mid-winter, on the coldest nights, the sanitary police corral the tramps here and in their lodging-houses and vaccinate them, despite their struggles and many oaths that they have recently been 'scraped.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public-health intervention used by officials as a preventive measure among transient populations; presented as routine sanitary policy in lodging-houses and station-houses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lodging-house classification by price and corresponding quality
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a wider gap between the 'hotel' that charges a quarter and the one that furnishes a bed for a dime; twenty-five-cent lodging-house, fifteen-cent, ten-cent, seven-cent, five-cent, three-cent — each price-point corresponds to progressively worse accommodations (private cubicles, bunks, canvas strips, bare floor, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses nightly price as a de facto standard to classify lodging-houses and predict conditions/risks: higher prices imply somewhat better privacy and amenities; lower prices correlate with crowding, filth, lack of lockers, and increased criminal influence. This classification functions as an evaluative rubric for assessing lodging-house severity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lodging-houses as nurseries of crime (official evaluation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The cheap lodging-houses ... have been stamped as nurseries of crime by the chief of the Secret Police; 'The ten-cent lodging-houses more than counterbalance the good done by the free reading-room, lectures, and all other agencies of reform. Such lodging-houses have caused more destitution, more beggary and crime than any other agency I know of.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Official evaluative judgment used to assess social impact of lodging-houses: inspectors and magistrates cite arrest records and case histories (e.g., numbers of young men recruited into petty crime) to substantiate the claim. Serves as a criterion when arguing for regulation or reform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stale-beer dives / two-cent restaurants: operational characterization
rubrics_metrics.description: Stale-beer dives (two-cent restaurants) sell doctored, unlicensed beer; sometimes a cup of 'coffee' and a stale roll for two cents; the privilege to sit or sleep in the premises goes with purchase; 'to the women ... the place is free.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes the business model and social role of stale-beer dives as part of trampdom: cheap intoxicants, places to sit/sleep, and a gateway into deeper vagrancy. This characterization functions as an evaluative standard to identify exploitative establishments and their social harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Police vagrancy/arrest practices and sentencing norm
rubrics_metrics.description: During raids ... 'Thirteen!' called the sergeant, 'Take them out. 'Revolvers' all but one. Good for six months on the island, the whole lot.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes the routine enforcement response: mass arrests for vagrancy, arraignment in police court, and a common sentencing outcome of six months on Blackwell's Island. Also notes repetition (same person may be sent twice in 24 hours) and political season modulation of enforcement/leniency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting lodgings as a homelessness metric
rubrics_metrics.description: According to the police figures, 4,974,025 separate lodgings were furnished last year by these dormitories ... adding the 147,634 lodgings furnished by the station-houses, the total of the homeless army was 5,121,659, an average of over fourteen thousand homeless men for every night in the year!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrates a method for quantifying homelessness by summing nightly lodgings provided by lodging-houses and stations over a year; used here as an official statistic to indicate scale and growth (increase over previous year).

rubrics_metrics.name: Political exploitation metric: lodging-houses as voter colonies
rubrics_metrics.description: About election time ... the lodging-houses come out strong on the side of the political boss who has the biggest 'barrel' ... the lodging-houses are his favorite recruiting ground.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluative claim that lodging-houses are used operationally by political machines to monetize and mobilize votes; cited as a factor obstructing reform and as a social harm metric (corruption of elections).

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualitative indicators of tenement squalor (descriptive checklist)
rubrics_metrics.description: Piles of rags, malodorous bones and musty paper; parlor and two pitch-dark coops called bedrooms; a broken stove with leaky pipe; one bed rooming six adults and five children; musty, torn wallpaper; kerosene lamp; crawling bugs in crust on floor; heaps of foul straw; babies dying from heat in unventilated rooms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author's descriptive inventory serves as a qualitative rubric for identifying dangerously unsanitary and overcrowded living units. These observable signs are presented as practical markers for inspectors, reformers, or reporters to recognize abusive housing conditions.
